theory.overview: Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS) are the two fundamental algorithms for traversing or searching graph/tree data structures. DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking (using a stack). BFS explores all neighbors at current depth before moving deeper (using a queue). Each has distinct properties: DFS uses less memory and finds paths quickly; BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

keyConcepts.name: DFS - Depth First
keyConcepts.description: Explore deep before wide. Uses stack (recursive or explicit). Good for: topological sort, detecting cycles, finding connected components.

keyConcepts.name: BFS - Breadth First
keyConcepts.description: Explore wide before deep. Uses queue. Guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs. Good for: shortest path, level-order traversal.

keyConcepts.name: Visited Set
keyConcepts.description: Track visited nodes to avoid cycles and redundant processing. Essential for both DFS and BFS.

keyConcepts.name: Time & Space Complexity
keyConcepts.description: Both O(V + E) time to visit all vertices and edges. DFS: O(h) space (h = height). BFS: O(w) space (w = max width).

complexity.dfsSpace: O(h) where h is max depth
complexity.bfsSpace: O(w) where w is max width

algorithmSteps.description: DFS: Start at A, push to stack. Stack = [A]
Pop A, mark visited. Push neighbors C, B onto stack.
Pop B (LIFO), mark visited. Push D, E onto stack.
Pop D. No unvisited neighbors. D is leaf node.
Pop E. Push F (only unvisited neighbor).
Now BFS: Start at A, enqueue. Queue = [A]
Dequeue A. Enqueue B, C. Level 0 complete.
Dequeue B. Enqueue D, E. Still processing level 1.
Dequeue C. Enqueue F. Level 1 complete.
